members.name: John Fogarty (founder, lead singer, chief songwriter)

podcast.title: Copyright Ownership Dispute
podcast.body: The copyrights to songs written by John Fogarty for Credence Clearwater Revival were transferred to Saul Zaentz, who ran the band's record label, Fantasy Records, as part of a contract dispute settlement. This led to a bizarre lawsuit where Fogarty was sued for plagiarizing himself. "Although John had written the songs for Credence, the copyrights, the ownership of the songs he had written, had been given over to a guy named Saul Zance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Heartland Rock Model
podcast.body: Credence Clearwater Revival is considered to have created the foundational model for Heartland Rock. Despite originating from the Bay Area in California rather than the Midwest, their music incorporated elements of blues, country, rock, and roots, which became hallmarks of the genre. "I think that Credence Clearwater Revival created the model for Heartland Rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 55 - Heartland Rock is about More than the Heartland

podcast.title: Noted Exception in "Depressed" Rock Scene
podcast.body: In his review of Elton John's 1970 debut, Los Angeles Times critic Robert Hilburn noted that the rock scene had been "rather depressed lately," with Credence Clearwater Revival being one of the few exceptions providing artistic substance amidst a period of "electronic noise" and "million sellers." "The fact is the rock scene has been rather depressed lately, except for the band, Credence Clearwater Revival, Joe Cocker and Leon Russell."

srcs.episode: Ep. 41 - The Impact of The Troubadour on 1970s Popular Culture

podcast.title: Populist Image
podcast.body: The band was viewed as a "band of the people," embodying populism by wearing work clothes like flannel and jeans, contrasting sharply with the rock star excess known from groups like Led Zeppelin or the Rolling Stones. This image set a precedent for future Heartland Rock artists. "They were considered a band of the people, populism in flannel and genes, and not the stars of the kind of the rock star excess that groups like Led Zeppelin or the Rolling Stones were known for."

xref.title: Plagiarism Lawsuit Against John Fogarty (1985)
xref.body: Saul Zaentz, who owned the copyrights to Credence Clearwater Revival's songs (including "Run Through the Jungle") through Fantasy Records, sued John Fogarty for plagiarism. Zaentz alleged that Fogarty's solo song "Old Man Down the Road" sounded too similar to "Run Through the Jungle," a song Zaentz owned the copyright to, despite Fogarty having written both. "While in Saul freaked out, got all bent out of shape, and then he sued John for plagiarism, alleging that a song on Center Field called Old Man Down the Road, which John owned, sounded just like an old CCR song called Run Through the Jungle, which Saul owned as the result of the contract dispute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Plagiarism Lawsuit for Self-Plagiarism (1985)
xref.body: John Fogarty, founder and chief songwriter for Credence Clearwater Revival, was sued for plagiarism in 1985 after releasing his solo album "Center Field." The lawsuit alleged that songs on his solo album, specifically "Old Man Down the Road," stole melodies from old CCR songs like "Run Through the Jungle," the copyrights of which were owned by Saul Zaentz of Fantasy Records, not Fogarty himself. "Then, in 1985, John released a solo record called Center Field and it too did very, very well. But then John was served with a lawsuit alleging plagiarism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Contract Dispute and Copyright Transfer
xref.body: John Fogarty had given ownership of his Credence Clearwater Revival songs to Saul Zaentz, who ran CCR's record label, Fantasy Records, in order to get out of his contract, indicating a strong animosity between them. "Although John had written the songs for Credence, the copyrights, the ownership of the songs he had written, had been given over to a guy named Saul Zance."
